title: Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams
text:
Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

An AI feature can save users time on a task, only for them to spend it checking the results. This practical audit helps product teams decide where AI earns its place and what users need to verify its output.

title: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
text:
Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology.

title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
text:

Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration.

title: Decision theatre or decision design?
text:
Decision theatre or decision design?

AI has made information easy, but it has not made decisions simple. As machines produce more than we can read, our job is shifting from building knowledge to owning decisions. Are we ready?

In a 2025 survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40% of US desk workers said they had received workslop in the previous month: AI-generated work that looks polished but does not move the task forward. Respondents reported spending nearly two hours, on average, dealing with each incident.

Imagine a team of ten, each receiving one piece of workslop a month. That is roughly 20 hours, more than two working days, spent cleaning up someone else’s shortcut.

We have never produced so much data, so many documents, decks and summaries. And we have never produced so much digital waste.

This is a productivity problem, but it is also a symptom.

The question is not how much faster we can produce something. It is how much extra work that production creates for everyone else, and who is left to decide what any of it means.

How did we get here?

For most of human history, change moved slowly. Roughly ten thousand years separated the birth of farming from industrialisation. Evolution had time to move from one stage to the next, across centuries and generations.

Then the interval shrank. Only about two centuries separated the first factories from the rise of service and knowledge economies.

And then it shrank again. In 1969, ARPANET connected its first computers: the beginning of the information society. Less than sixty years later, AI agents use the knowledge we put online to make recommendations and, more and more… decisions.

Think about what we did in those sixty years. We created the bits. We built digital worlds and a digital culture. We ran digitalisation programmes. We put books online with Project Gutenberg, information online with Wikipedia. We worked hard to make information accessible and ubiquitous, on every channel, for everyone.

Without knowing it, we were laying the foundation for an artificial form of intelligence to learn from our human-built infrastructure, and to work on top of it.

The information society was basically the training ground for AI. Our knowledge is now the bridge between the old, human-driven world and a new, AI-empowered one.

This compression raises a pressing question.
How quickly can people, organisations and institutions adapt?

Does more information make us wiser?

Not on its own. And we have known that for a long time.

In information management, one of the best-known frameworks is the DIKW pyramid: Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom. It is usually credited to Russell Ackoff, who formalised it at the end of the 1980s.

The logic is simple:

  • Data: the raw elements. Facts and signals with no context.
  • Information: data that has been processed and organised.
  • Knowledge: information that has been interpreted and put to use.
  • Wisdom: knowledge that allows judgement.

Each level is built on the one below, but the relationship only works one way. As Steyn puts it, wisdom is always knowledge, but knowledge is not always wisdom. Every level is a subset of the one beneath it.

In 1987, Milan Zeleny proposed the same four levels in a language that organisations understand much better:

  • Know-nothing: data
  • Know-what: information
  • Know-how: knowledge
  • Know-why: wisdom

Read it from the bottom up: each level is built on the one below, but no amount of data adds up to wisdom on its own.

For Zeleny, managing efficiently means knowing how to do things. Managing effectively means knowing what to do. Managing wisely means knowing why. And wisdom goes one step further: it is what lets us compare and judge our know-how and our know-what.

I first wrote about this back in 2013, on LegoViews. Back then, the challenge was getting organisations to make time for that reflection.
Today it is harder. AI hands us endless know-what and know-how in seconds, and reflection, the step that turns them into a shared know-why, is exactly the one we are tempted to skip.

Here is the point that matters most today. Wisdom comes from knowledge, but it is not a sum of knowledge.

Adding knowledge to knowledge does not make wisdom. Processing more information does not make us wiser.

What does AI know, and what doesn’t it?

AI is extraordinary at the bottom of the pyramid. It processes data at a scale no team could match, and it turns that data into know-how: summaries, drafts, analyses, code.

What it cannot settle for us is which problem deserves attention, whose interests should count, and whether we should act on its answer.

These questions depend on context. They put the output into a broader frame: what we are trying to achieve, under which constraints, and why it matters. That frame is where knowledge gets judged.

The worrying part is how many people now trust good-looking information, mistake it for wisdom, and pass it on. Especially in the domains where critical thinking is the whole job.

And even the know-how needs checking. Large language models still add unsupported claims when they summarise a document they were given. On Vectara’s hallucination leaderboard, which tests this, rates in 2026 run from 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries, depending on the model. These are task-specific figures, not universal error rates. But they show how hard it is to rely on AI output that nobody reads closely.

So we have a base of data and good-looking information, produced at a volume that no human can manage.

What are we losing?

For most of my career, the journey from data to judgement had its own pace. And it was work, real work.

We collected an adequate amount of data. We prioritised. We designed studies around sampling and around the constraints we had: time, resources, our ability to analyse, the tools at hand. The constraints forced us to choose, and choosing forced us to think.

Today we are in the middle of a data feast. We access more and more data not because we need it, but because we can.

Slowly, we are creating working conditions in which there is less room to think, prioritise, sequence and distil. Less room for intentionality.

The philosopher John Searle described intentionality as the mind’s capacity to be about something (Intentionality, 1983). In organisations, it takes a more practical shape: the deliberate decision to focus attention and action on a clearly defined purpose. What we are trying to achieve, why it matters, and how our choices serve it.

It is made of a few simple things:

  • Awareness: knowing where we are and what we are looking at.
  • Context: understanding the situation and its variables.
  • Prioritisation: directing attention to what has the most impact.
  • Distillation: separating value from noise.

Without it, we stay in the noise. We consume data because we do not know where we are going, or where we should focus.

All the narratives are about speed. We are omitting the craft.

We stopped trusting the process because we only look at the output. But an output without a process is a simulacrum: something that looks good and has no substance.

What gives value to data and knowledge is not the shape of the output. It is the process that generated it and gave it substance.

Who decides?

AI can do a lot, and it does some things better than we do. But there is one thing it cannot do: be held accountable.

The idea is much older than generative AI. A slide said to come from a 1979 IBM internal training warned that “a computer can never be held accountable”, and concluded that a computer should therefore never make a management decision. The original has never been found in IBM’s archives, but the principle has aged remarkably well (more here).

Nearly fifty years later, regulation gives human oversight a concrete organisational form. Article 26(2) of the EU AI Act asks deployers of high-risk AI systems to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, and to give them the support they need.

So let’s be clear.

An insurance claim. A loan. A place at a school. Access to benefits.

AI can support every one of these decisions. It can sort the files, flag the risks, summarise the evidence. But these decisions must not become a way for organisations to hide responsibility behind a system.

These decisions affect people’s fundamental rights. Behind each one there must be a human with a name, a role, the responsibility, the authority and the skills to make the decision, stand by it, defend it, and answer for the consequences.

That does not relieve the organisation of responsibility for the system, the workflow or the conditions in which that person is expected to decide.

AI can inform. It cannot own.

This is where the paradox emerges: we have the illusion that we are outsourcing more and more work. In reality, our job is becoming that of the AI supervisor: the person in charge of making AI-enabled decisions.

In one sentence: after we digitalised knowledge and built all the infrastructure, our role is no longer only to build knowledge. It is also to take responsibility for how that knowledge informs decisions.

We are moving from the information society to an age of accountability, where we need to embrace our humanity to make decisions about other humans.

Decision theatre or decision design?

Responsible AI needs humans in the loop. That much is agreed. But a human in the loop is not enough on their own.

Put a disengaged, overloaded or alienated person in front of an AI output and you get decision theatre: the illusion that a decision happened when it did not. Someone clicked “approve”. Nobody decided.

We have a decision-making crisis, and more AI output will deepen it unless something changes. Most organisations lack a decision-making operational layer to support the people who must make the decisions.

A real decision needs three conditions:

  • Skills: the competence and training to read the context, the variables and the pre-digested input, and to tell a valid answer from a well-formatted one.
  • Authority: a name, a role and a position that allow the person to override the AI, and the responsibility to own the result.
  • Process: workflows designed to empower decision makers, with the right information, tools and time, and without drowning them in decision fatigue.

Take one away and the decision collapses into theatre.

Who holds the judgement?

It is tempting to map Zeleny’s forms of knowing onto an organisational chart: leadership decides why, management decides what, operations deliver how. But Zeleny was describing forms of knowing, not ranks of people.

The mistake is to confuse the authority to make a decision with the knowledge needed to make it well. A frontline worker may have no say in strategy, yet can be the first to notice when a process is failing or a case does not fit the rules. Research on digitalised frontline work shows that this tacit knowledge and discretion still matter, even where systems automate parts of the process.

Automate that work without asking what judgement it holds, and the organisation loses more than a task.

Imagine a caseworker reviewing benefit claims flagged by an AI system.

In the theatre version, they get hundreds of cases a day. They see a risk score and two buttons. They have no time to open the file, and overriding the system needs their manager’s sign-off. They approve what the machine suggests. On paper, a human was in the loop.

In the designed version, they get fewer cases, prioritised by uncertainty. They see the sources behind each score and the points where the system is least confident. They can override it, and they record why. Their overrides go back to the team that runs the system, so recurring problems can be investigated and corrected.

Same person. Same AI. A completely different decision.

This is where design enters the scene. Somebody has to design these decision-making workflows: to enable, and indeed empower, humans to decide, and to avoid both decision fatigue and decision theatre.

What skills will the human in the loop need?

If humans are expected to own AI-supported decisions, we need to be clear about what that responsibility requires. We need humans who think as humans, not as machines.

What does that mean?

It means humans who understand the problem, the context and the domain. It means humans who understand the AI output and the process that produced it. It means humans who can separate the validity of the content from the polish of the form.

Three families of skills will matter most.

  • Critical judgement: being sceptical, spotting errors, asking where a claim comes from, and noticing what is missing as well as what is there.
  • Sense-making: taking the knowledge we have built and organising it into structures that increase accuracy, logic, relationships and reliability.
  • Human skills: the so-called soft skills, and the hardest to delegate. Empathy for the person on the other side of the decision. The courage to disagree with the machine. The integrity to sign your name under the result.

None of these is new. What is new is that they are no longer a nice-to-have on top of the “real” work.

They are the work.

How do we teach people to decide?

If these skills are the work, we need to teach them differently. People reviewing AI-supported decisions need practice in judging incomplete evidence, recognising exceptions, understanding the context and rules that apply, and explaining what they decided and why. Without that preparation, we risk creating a new assembly line: people processing recommendations and carrying responsibility for decisions they barely have time to examine.

This means rethinking curricula, in schools, universities and workplaces, around a few plain questions:

  • How do we analyse data to tell the what from the why?
  • How do we read a situation as a system, with its relationships, feedback loops and unintended consequences?
  • How do we decide under uncertainty, and how do we stand by that decision?
  • How do we notice when we are being asked to perform a decision rather than make one?

This is why we need much more teaching in complexity theory and systems thinking. Not as niche electives for a few specialists, but as the foundation for anyone who will sign their name under an AI-enabled decision.

In one word: we need to teach judgement.

What’s next

For years, many of us watched design thinking turn into design doing: more output, faster, with less and less time to think. AI can now do the doing faster than any of us.

This is the crossroads.

One road leads to more of the same. More outputs, more workslop, more decisions that only look like decisions.

The other road brings thinking back to the centre. Framing the problem. Understanding the context. Prioritising. Designing the process that turns AI output into a decision a human can own. This is design thinking applied to the most human act of all: deciding about other humans.

References

  • Ackoff, R. L. (1989). From data to wisdom. Journal of Applied Systems Analysis, 16, 3–9.
  • Searle, J. (1983). Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind. Cambridge University Press.
  • Zeleny, M. (1987). Management support systems: towards integrated knowledge management. Human Systems Management, 7(1), 59–70.

title: AI is the new old design material
text:
AI is the new old design material

Creative makers and builders have always learned their medium by working with it, from grinding pigments to HTML. Models are the next material, and you need to learn them by building.

The field keeps arguing about whether designers should code, as if that question were new.

It’s not new.

Art and design have always been taught through materials, going back centuries.

In the 1390s, the painter Cennino Cennini wrote a handbook that’s still translated today on grinding pigments, and that history still runs through my own family as builders and creators. My mother, Jean Neeman, ground her own pigments as a conservator for the Los Angeles Museum of Art, the Getty and Hearst Castle, and I watched her repair Chinese statues that were over 600 years old with original materials to restore history.

She lived that craft, as I wrote in Everything I Know About UX I Learned From My Parents. I learned print through paste up, developing film for prints, and running film output.

I understand that knowing the material is a timeless need, and most designers I meet don’t understand it, because their tools hide it. We need to respect it as part of the craft.

The reality is that visual tools like Figma and Sketch are an abstraction, and real craft happens in the final mile, working with the material. Great designers have always used the materials they had, and I’ve always written code as part of the job to understand mine.

On the web, that meant HTML, CSS, Javascript and whatever else that made it work. Artificial intelligence is the new material, teaching the same lesson faster.

The designers doing the strongest work with models run them and read the output. That takes sampling code: a loop asking one question over and over until the model’s habits show.

Study the Bauhaus Workshops

In April 1919, Walter Gropius published the founding manifesto of the Bauhaus, and its demand was direct.

As art historian Magdalena Droste explains in The Bauhaus Manifesto, Gropius told architects, sculptors, and painters to turn to the crafts. The curriculum ended in a list of workshops. Students learned wood, metal, glass, and weaving by cutting, bending, and threading them.

Josef Albers made the point with almost nothing. In his preliminary course, Droste notes, students had to make a flat sheet of paper stand on its own, or bend a straight wire until it held its shape.

A drawing can suggest a chair, but only the wood can tell you where it will split.

That habit produced the school’s best-known work. Marcel Breuer headed the carpentry workshop and bent tubular steel into chairs, and Herbert Bayer went on to run the printing and advertising workshop.

They knew their materials because they had worked them. Every new medium since has sent designers back to a bench of some kind, and the last two benches have been made of code.

Hand-Code 1990s Web Pages

The web forced the same return, and it started with a blank file.

In the mid-1990s, the design tool for the web was a text editor: Notepad on Windows, SimpleText on the Mac. You typed tags, saved the file, and reloaded the browser to see what you’d made. My earliest web credit, the Oliver North home page, came out of that era.

Dedicated tools followed quickly, and each one moved the designer a step further from the markup:

  • BBEdit (1992), a Mac text editor that added HTML tools in 1994.
  • HoTMetaL (1994), an early HTML editor that showed where each tag began and ended.
  • PageMill (1995), Adobe’s visual editor for print designers.
  • FrontPage (1995), a visual editor that Microsoft bought in early 1996.
  • HomeSite (1996), a Windows editor built for people who wanted to write the HTML themselves.
  • Dreamweaver (1997), Macromedia’s visual editor.

The designers who got the most out of the visual editors still opened the code underneath. They trusted the canvas only after checking the page in more than one browser.

A visual editor showed one browser’s best case, and the markup showed the rest.

In 2000, John Allsopp wrote A Dao of Web Design for A List Apart, arguing that the control designers knew in print was a product of the printed page’s limits.

Ten years later, ethan marcotte opened Responsive Web Design with a quote from Allsopp. He built a sample page on a fluid grid with flexible images and media queries, then showed the layout changing shape as the window narrowed.

Responsive design came out of a designer’s style sheet, and no mockup would have found it.

Five years later, Frank Chimero gave the idea a name in The Web’s Grain, writing that “every material has a grain, including the web.” He argued that the field’s best techniques grew out of that grain, and that sites built against it come out fragile and awkward.

Test Model Output Variation

Models break the mockup in a new way. A static screen shows one answer, chosen by the designer and usually the good one. A model returns a different answer each time, and that spread is the thing you’re designing for. Call the chosen answer the one-sample mockup: a screen built around the output the model gives on its best day.

In legal tech, where wedesigned search and summarization, every summary in a mockup was correct, because a designer wrote it.

  • In 2017, Lars Erik Holmquist argued in Intelligence on Tap: Artificial Intelligence as a New Design Material that designers should treat the technology as a material with its own limits.
  • In UX Design Innovation: Challenges for Working with Machine Learning as a Design Material (2017), Graham Dove and colleagues surveyed UX practitioners. They suggested that machine learning had seen little design innovation, possibly because it was a new and difficult material.
  • Qian Yang’s 2020 dissertation at Carnegie Mellon University, Profiling Artificial Intelligence as a Material for User Experience Design, went further. It traced those difficulties to two roots: uncertainty about what a system can do, and the complexity of what it might output.
A mockup is one sample, and the product is the distribution.

The Doherty Threshold entry on UX Guidelines, my own reference site, puts the point where software starts to feel conversational under 400 milliseconds. A static frame can’t show a four-second wait.

Bret Victor built a whole talk, Inventing on Principle (2012), around the idea that creators need an immediate connection to what they create. You find the spread, the misses, and the delays only by running the model again and again.

Code Prototypes Against Models

Josh Clark tied the two eras together in his 2018 talk The New Design Material, calling machine learning “a design material in the same way that HTML and CSS is.”

In Addressing UX Practitioners’ Challenges in Designing ML Applications (2023), K. J. Kevin Feng and David W. McDonald of the University of Washington ran a study with 27 UX practitioners. Each got a tool to build and test simple models while designing an app.

Hands-on experimentation helped them match model behavior to user goals, invent interface features for correcting the model, and spot ethical risks. One participant explained that without testing, you don’t know “how often or in what ways it’s going to error.”

The authors located the bottleneck in fabrication, the stage where models get made, because designers are usually kept away from it. Their tool needed no code at all.

Today, for language models, a few lines of code are the shortest route to the same hands-on access. Geoffrey Litt saw it coming in Malleable software in the age of LLMs (2023), arguing that language models would let ordinary users build small tools from scratch.

Designers have kept themselves at arm’s length from the material, and that distance is the bottleneck they can no longer ignore.

That distance is closing. Figma’s 2026 AI report found that the share of designers participating in development doubled in a year, from 21% to 41%.

Tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Figma Make let a designer describe a prototype, wire it to a live model, and watch what breaks in a single sitting.

Not every designer agrees that code belongs in the job. Alan Cooper wrote in Should Designers Code? (2017) that “coding is not a skill necessary to be a top notch interaction designer.”

Karri Saarinen of Linear warned in Design Is More Than Code (2025) that production-first habits can erode the thinking behind a design. Both warnings are about code that ships.

Sampling code gets thrown away the same afternoon, and its only job is to show you the material.

Write AI Evaluation Sets

Sampling code doesn’t need to ship. It works like a test bench, and its most valuable output is a record of every case where the model broke the design. Wood doesn’t change its grain overnight, but a model can change with a single provider update.

Engineers already have a name for this file: an evaluation set. Designers are well placed to write it. They know which failures users notice first, like the answer that runs past the edge of its card or the wrong date stated with total confidence.

A design tuned to last month’s model can fail without a single pixel moving.

Four habits turn the record into working practice:

  • Call the model directly. Ask Claude Code or Cursor for a script that sends real product inputs to the model and prints the answers, and read them before you draw a screen.
  • Run each prompt 50 times. Sort the answers by length, tone, and accuracy, then design for the longest and the most wrong rather than the typical one.
  • Bring the spread to review. Put the two worst of the 50 answers beside the mockup in design review, and decide together which ones the screen must survive.
  • Save failures as test cases. Keep every output that broke a layout or misled a user in a shared file, so engineering reruns it whenever the model or prompt changes.

Run the Model First

Gropius moved students out of drawing rooms because drawings hid what materials would do.

Designers on the early web learned the same thing in a text editor, and Marcotte proved it with a working page. The debate over whether designers should code has always been a debate about the material and how close designers can get to it.

For artificial intelligence products, the material is the model’s behavior across thousands of inputs. You won’t find it in a frame on a canvas. You find it by running the model, reading everything that comes back, and keeping the failures somewhere the team can see them.

These days I describe my job as building, and that’s the reason: I can’t design how a model-backed product works until I’ve watched the model work.

Next time your team reviews an artificial intelligence feature, skip the one-sample mockup. Run the prompt 50 times, bring the worst answer to the review, and design the screen that survives it. Notice which answers the whole room argues about, because those are the cases a static mockup was hiding.

That’s the workshop now, and the door is open to anyone willing to write a few lines of sampling code.

title: The AI mind tax that afflicts those who use AI best
text:
The AI mind tax that afflicts those who use AI best

AI was supposed to make work easier, but for the people who use it most, it just became a different kind of work, and a whole lot of exhaustion.

The promise of the tech was that AI would make work easier, and, sure, in plenty of ways it came true, but for the people using it the hardest, it created a second job nobody considered, managing the pile of tools that now does the work for you.

The folks who stay sharp hold onto what the machine still can’t do for them, their judgment, their ability to work with other people, and some grip on where the work actually stands, but there’s a price to pay for that.

We’re not talking about just one burnt out person, because nobody was hired for this. The title still says marketer, or designer, or founder. The job shifted to keeping a dozen disconnected machines pointed in the same direction, and the whole industry is pretending that isn’t the work.

The people embracing AI the right way, learning the tools, wiring them into everything, getting genuinely good, are the ones getting buried, because being good at this now means being the one who holds it all together. A recent benchmark from CMO Huddles and Benchmarkit shows why. 98 percent of marketing teams use AI somewhere, and only 3 percent have connected it across their work. The companies didn’t build the connective layer, so the capable people became it.

In a research project I’ve been working with CMOs, I was chatting with a marketer I know who has been in the tech industry for almost twenty years. Her career has spanned some big tech names you would definitely know and these days she runs pretty much all the marketing at a startup by herself.

As we discussed the evolution of marketing and the marketing executive today, it became very clear that she’s about as deep into AI as anyone I’ve met. She is wired into every tool she touches, running most of her day through Claude and ChatGPT. She can spin up a user survey, analyze it, write the launch plan, and build the assets herself. All the stuff that used to take a whole team.

If AI was built to make anyone’s job easier, it was built for her.

I figured, if anything, that AI had simplified her life exponentially and that she’d admit as much. Instead she told me she feels like she’s “melting on the inside.”

The tools aren’t the problem. There are just so many of them, all living in different places, and she’s the only thing holding them together. Figma, the CRM, Claude, ChatGPT, Slack, each one its own window with its own half-finished conversation, and she’s the one keeping track of which idea she had where.

She called it a real tax and toll. She also said she wouldn’t give a single one of these tools back.

And that job is exhausting.

She was not an outlier. One fractional CMO I talked to runs marketing for a whole stack of startups at once, each with its own set of tools, its own logins, its own AI baked into the CRM and the design software and everything else, and she is the only human carrying context from one to the next.

Another person I spoke to runs a team at a big company where everyone has quietly built their own personal pile of AI agents, each one tuned to how that person works, so when someone leaves, the knowledge of how any of it fits together walks out with them.

Different companies, different budgets, same situations. The person in the middle is the integration layer, and the integration layer is tired.

The fatigue is real

What she described as “melting” is a documented, measurable thing. For better or worse, the research on it was pretty disturbingly long before any of us used a chatbot.

Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke found that it takes about twenty-three minutes to fully get your focus back after a single interruption.

Similarly, Rohan Narayana Murty, Sandeep Dadlani and Rajath B. Das, studying workers across three Fortune 500 companies, found that people toggle between different applications and websites around twelve hundred times a day.

Cornell’s Ellis Idea Lab, working with Qatalog, found it takes nine and a half minutes just to get back into a workflow after switching apps, that forty-five percent of workers say too many apps make them less productive, and that nearly half admit they make actual mistakes because they can’t keep track of what’s happening across all their tools.

That was the cost of switching between dumb apps that just sat there and waited for you. Then every one of those apps grew its own AI.

As the switching multiplied, every tool became two things to keep track of, the tool and the AI living inside it. The marketer I spoke to isn’t just bouncing between Figma and the CRM and Slack anymore. She’s bouncing between Figma’s AI and the CRM’s AI and Claude and ChatGPT, each one a separate conversation, each one knowing nothing about the others, each one needing to be caught up.

The one thing none of these tools reliably does is hold the thread for you.

Rifat Mehreen Amin and her colleagues, studying how people actually use AI chatbots, gave the problem a name, context fragmentation, and watched people cope with it by copying pieces of one conversation into another by hand, stitching the results back together across sessions, rebuilding their own mental map every time they came back.

You become the only part of the system that remembers what you were doing in the other four windows, which is why, at the end of a day like that, you feel like you’re melting on the inside. It also means you are the only one who knows where any of it stands.

When all the context lives in your head, explaining to your manager or your team where the work actually is becomes its own task, and nobody else can pick it up without you.

You turned into the glue

The reason all of this lands on her and not on the machines is simple. The machines don’t talk to each other, so she has to. Every tool she uses has become its own little walled garden with its own AI inside it.

Figma’s AI knows about the file she’s in and nothing else. The CRM’s AI knows about campaigns and nothing else. Claude knows about the conversation she’s having with Claude. None of them know about any of the others.

Connectors are starting to change that at the edges. You can wire Figma or a CRM into Claude so it can reach into them directly. Xinyi Hou and her colleagues, in a survey of the connector landscape, found that even with a shared standard for these integrations, stitching tools together remains fragmented, and the connections mostly run one way, into whichever assistant she has made the hub. The other tools still sit in their own corners.

She is still the one deciding what connects to what, and carrying across by hand whatever doesn’t.

Jan-Philipp Steghöfer studied how professionals actually use AI tools across their real workflows and found that the most persistent frustration was almost never the AI’s ability. It was the breaks between the tools, each one useful on its own, none able to hand off to the next, so the person in the middle rebuilds the context from scratch every time and carries it across by hand. One worker in his study described finishing in one AI tool and manually moving the output into the next just to keep going.

The marketer I talked to does the same thing, having ChatGPT write a summary of one conversation so she can paste it into Claude to start another. She has become the connective tissue between systems that were supposed to connect themselves.

The cruel part is that all of that burden on your shoulders feels productive. It feels like work getting done.

The research keeps finding that the feeling and the reality don’t match.

The cleanest proof comes from METR, a nonprofit that ran a careful randomized controlled trial on experienced developers doing real work in codebases they knew inside out. Going in, the developers expected AI to speed them up by around a quarter. They did the work, and afterward they still believed it had made them about twenty percent faster.

When the researchers measured the actual time, the developers had been nineteen percent slower with the AI than without it. The gap between how fast they felt and how fast they were ran close to forty points, and it held even after they’d lived through the slowdown themselves.

That gap is the whole danger of the mind tax. You cannot feel it while it is happening. You feel busy, you feel capable, you feel like you are getting an enormous amount done, and some of that is true.

Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye found the same thing over eight months of watching people adopt AI at a tech company. The tools intensified the work instead of shrinking it. People took on more, moved faster, and stretched the day longer, largely because AI made doing more feel possible.

Instead of the rest or deeper thinking you’d expect, the time it saved resulted in more work, more tools to run, and more threads to manage.

It comes for your best people first

The cruel joke of the mind tax is who it hits hardest. You would think it’s the people just dabbling with AI who get worn down the most, but the reality is that it’s the people who dove in head first.

Julie Bedard, Matthew Kropp, Megan Hsu and their colleagues at Boston Consulting Group studied nearly fifteen hundred workers and found that productivity climbs as you add AI tools, right up until about the third one. After that it falls. The workers running four or more tools at once were getting less done, making more errors, and reporting more of the exact buzzing, fried feeling the marketer described. The fatigue came from overseeing the AI, not from handing work to it.

All the watching and checking and correcting, and the holding of everything in your head at once, is its own kind of labor, and the people doing the most of it were the heaviest users, the ones who leaned in hardest.

The study found the highest rates were in marketing, which is to say, in people exactly like my CMO friend.

The management version of this is worse than the productivity one. Those same researchers found that workers who weren’t fried intended to leave their jobs at a rate of about one in four. Among the workers who were fried, it rose to one in three.

The Upwork Research Institute found the same thing from another angle, that the most productive AI users, the ones getting the biggest gains, were also the most burned out, with 88 percent of them reporting burnout and roughly twice the likelihood of looking for the exit.

This mental tax seriously wears out your best people and then pushes them out the door. The problem is, of course, that these are the exact people you cannot afford to lose.

What should worry anyone who does this work for a living is the impact to a person’s mind underneath it all. Nataliya Kosmyna and her team at the MIT Media Lab wired people up and watched their brains while they wrote, some on their own, some leaning on AI. The heavy AI users showed weaker neural engagement, remembered less of what they’d produced, and felt less ownership of it.

The researchers called what builds up “cognitive debt,” the brain quietly doing less of its own work once a machine is there to do it.

Michael Gerlich found a matching pattern in a study of six hundred and sixty-six people. The more someone relied on AI, the weaker their critical thinking scored, and the thing connecting the two was cognitive offloading, the habit of handing your thinking to the tool. The effect was steepest in the heaviest and youngest users. Gerlich is careful that this is a correlation and not proof that AI caused the decline, and that caution is fair. The direction of it still lines up with what everyone living in these tools already feels.

Put the pieces together and the mind tax stops looking like plain tiredness. The thing getting taxed is judgment.

The more of the thinking you hand off, the less of it you are doing, and the less sharp you get at the one part of the job a machine still cannot do for you.

That is a genuinely terrible tradeoff. When it comes down to it, your judgment is the only thing you were ever really being paid for.

The new job is quietly eating the old one, and nobody has said so out loud.

A room with one voice in it

When I asked that marketer what she missed most, she avoided any mention of the AI tools in her arsenal, and focused entirely on teamwork and collaboration. The whiteboard, the ten people around a table, the coworker who could absorb her idea and say, in so many words, that it was wrong.

What she has now is a one-way screen. She does the work alone, runs it past an assistant that agrees with her, and then launches it.

The collaborator got replaced by something that never pushes back.

Myra Cheng, Dan Jurafsky and their colleagues at Stanford tested eleven leading AI models and found they affirmed what the user was doing about forty-nine percent more often than a human would, including in cases where the user was describing something deceptive or harmful. Worse, when people took interpersonal problems to a sycophantic model, a single conversation left them more convinced they were right and less willing to repair the situation and people liked it. They trusted the agreeable model more, which is exactly why companies have every reason to keep building it that way.

This is baked into how these systems are made. Anthropic’s own researchers, led by Mrinank Sharma and Ethan Perez, showed that the leading assistants are systematically sycophantic, because the training rewards it.

People reward the answer that flatters them over the one that corrects them, every time. Train a machine on that mentality and you get a world-class suck-up.

Even the humans overseeing the training, and the models built to imitate those humans, preferred the convincing wrong answer to the accurate inconvenient one a meaningful share of the time.

This dismantles what actually made the work good. Jan-Philipp Steghöfer’s study found that the single-user model of these tools substitutes a private conversation with the AI for the collaborative one with the team, the back-and-forth where people surface each other’s blind spots, challenge the weak idea, and build a shared understanding of why the thing is the way it is.

The team inherits the finished artifact but not the argument that should have shaped it. Our marketer friend felt the same loss. She said that when a team spends half an hour in a room on a problem, you get ten different minds pulling at it. With AI, you get one, and it’s pulling in whatever direction you already were.

The thing that used to make people good at this work was friction, the colleague who caught the mistake, the review that stung, the question you hadn’t thought to ask. Trade all of that for a tool that agrees with you, and the cost isn’t only time and focus.

The real loss is what was keeping your judgment honest.

Somebody has to pay for it

I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to think I’m making a case against AI and I’m not. The marketer I talked to would be the first to tell you that. She loves these tools. She said, more than once, that she wouldn’t give a single one of them back, that the amount she can do now would have taken a whole team the old way.

The gains are real. The tax is just the price nobody understood or identified when she started down this path.

Let’s be clear, it is a real price.

Add up everything we’ve walked through and you get the same result in three different outputs. There’s the work of running the tools, the context carried by hand from one window to the next. There’s the slow erosion of the thinking you stop doing because the machine is there to do it. There’s the quiet of working alone with something that only ever agrees with you.

This all comes down to one person standing in the middle of all the tools, holding it all together.

This is really a design problem.

Right now the human is the integration layer, the memory, the quality check, the only thing in the whole setup capable of saying “no, that’s wrong.”

We built a dozen brilliant tools and skipped the part that connects them, carries the thread, or pushes back. The work John Dubois, Chandra Shukla, and Kay Youngstrom from EY have done on redesigning jobs around AI makes the case that the win comes from augmentation, designing work so the tools sharpen human judgment instead of burying it. That is a thing to build, not a thing a person should have to white-knuckle their way through alone.

We need to embrace the idea that the job changed. Being good at this work, today, means being good at orchestration, at judgment, at holding a team together while the machines do the production. Create a name for that job, hire for it, build the day around it, and the tax gets smaller. Pretend the job is still what it used to be, and it keeps coming out of the person.

The reason to build it is that the one job that we could truly own, and still can, is judgment.

Knowing what’s good, knowing what’s missing, knowing when the confident answer is confidently wrong.

Peter Klein calls this the paradox of automation. The more AI takes over the routine work, the more valuable human judgment becomes, and at the same time the fewer chances people get to build it, because judgment is grown through exactly the hands-on work the machine is now doing.

Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic puts the same idea more bluntly. When machines do the thinking, humans have to do more of the judging. The mind tax is dangerous because it eats that capacity first. It buries the one thing you cannot afford to lose under the management of everything else.

So our marketer friend keeps going. She does the work of ten people, and then she does the work of managing the machines that do the work of ten people, and at the end of the day she feels like she’s melting on the inside.

The tools keep getting upgraded.

She’s still running on the same single brain she started with. Until someone designs for that, instead of around it, the tax comes out of her.

The tax will always come out of the person.

References and further reading

The fatigue is real

  • Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke, “The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress” (University of California, Irvine, 2008). The research on how long it takes to recover focus after an interruption.
  • “How Much Time and Energy Do We Waste Toggling Between Applications?” (Harvard Business Review, 2022). The study of workers across three Fortune 500 companies toggling around twelve hundred times a day.
  • Cornell’s Ellis Idea Lab, with Qatalog, “Workgeist Report ‘21” (2021). On the time lost and mistakes made switching between too many tools.
  • Rifat Mehreen Amin, Alperen Adatepe, Daniela Fernandes, Daniel Buschek, and Andreas Butz, “Conversations in Space: Non-Linear LLM Interaction in Everyday Use” (2026). On context fragmentation and how people carry it across AI chats by hand.

You turned into the glue

  • Jan-Philipp Steghöfer, “Faster than the Team, Faster than the Customer: Tool Integration, Collaboration, and Organisational Lag in AI-Assisted RE” (2026). On tool integration, not capability, as the binding constraint, and the human bridging the breaks.
  • Xinyi Hou, Yanjie Zhao, Shenao Wang, and Haoyu Wang, “Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions” (2025). On how, even with a shared standard for connectors, stitching AI tools together remains fragmented.
  • METR, “Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity” (2025). The randomized trial finding developers nineteen percent slower with AI while feeling faster.
  • Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye, “AI Doesn’t Reduce Work, It Intensifies It” (Harvard Business Review, 2026). On how AI expands the pace, scope, and hours of work rather than shrinking it.

It comes for your best people first

  • Julie Bedard, Matthew Kropp, Megan Hsu, and colleagues, “When Using AI Leads to ‘Brain Fry’” (Boston Consulting Group, in Harvard Business Review, 2026). On productivity peaking at three AI tools, and the fatigue and attrition that follow.
  • Upwork Research Institute, “From Burnout to Balance: AI-Enhanced Work Models” (2024). On the most productive AI users reporting the most burnout and the highest intent to quit.
  • Nataliya Kosmyna and colleagues, “Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt When Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing” (MIT Media Lab, 2026). On the measurable cognitive cost of offloading thinking to AI.
  • Michael Gerlich, “AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking” (Societies, 2025). On the correlation between heavy AI reliance and weaker critical thinking.

A room with one voice in it

  • Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Pranav Khadpe, Sunny Yu, Dyllan Han, and Dan Jurafsky, “Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence” (Science, 2026). On AI affirming users far more than humans do, and what that does to judgment.
  • Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Ethan Perez, and colleagues, “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models” (Anthropic, 2023). On how training rewards agreement over accuracy.

Somebody has to pay for it

  • John Dubois, Chandra Shukla, and Kay Youngstrom, “How to Redesign Work Around Human Skills in the Age of AI” (EY, 2026). On augmentation, designing work so AI sharpens human judgment rather than burying it.
  • Peter G. Klein, “AI and Human Judgment: Why People Still Matter” (Baylor University, Hankamer School of Business, 2026). On the paradox of automation and why judgment grows scarcer as it grows more valuable.
  • Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, “How AI Is Changing Decision Making in Organizations” (Forbes, 2026). On why, as machines do more of the thinking, humans have to do more of the judging.

title: Why are we cloning Photoshop?
text:
Why are we cloning Photoshop?

AI is making it easy to recreate professional tools. I suspect there’s a bigger opportunity being overlooked.

October saw the release of PhotoCraft, an open-source Photoshop clone built with AI that had a similar capability set, but without Adobe Creative Cloud’s exorbitant monthly price tag.

Building software with AI has become so cheap that a complex product which would have typically taken a large team to develop, can now be spun up for a fraction of the cost by a lone developer and a band of AI agents.

Even in an age where we can use AI directly in creative tasks to instantly generate designs and imagery, there’s still excitement around having tools that enable creatives to retain tight control to build out their vision.

So a cloned Photoshop solves the price problem, but if we still want to retain creative control we have to ask ourselves: do we all still need Photoshop’s way of working in the first place?

Just give me the outcome I want

Let’s take the example of a marketer who infrequently creates polished instructional product videos. They want their video edits to look professional, and need the ability to retain fine-grained creative control so that they can tweak and adjust timing, colour grading and titling to match their vision. But due to this not being the mainstay of their role, they may not want to navigate the complexities of a full editing tool like Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve.

This group of users that might find their needs met by a simpler, more convenient offering, can be referred to as overserved. The Christensen Institute’s disruptive innovation framework identifies this as a potential segment open to new offerings.

Applying a jobs-to-be-done lens further offers a real-world perspective. It’s context that very much differentiates the marketer in a start-up who wants a high-quality video from the ad agency video editor that produces edits on a daily basis. Both of these users want creative control, however one will be less likely to invest time in learning and mastering a tool for which they will use intermittently.

The marketer may not want to master a new product, but they also don’t want to relinquish creative decisions to an agent. They may use an agent to form a rough cut, but have a clear vision to evoke a specific feeling in their audience, and directly editing the video themselves makes this easier to achieve than describing it in a prompt.

Build around the work, not the tools

Apps that place the job to be done at the centre of the experience, whilst considering the user’s context and reducing the complexity of the tool’s mental model make for some really interesting value propositions.

Apps like Descript and Riverside allow video and audio editing not just through a traditional timeline, but through a transcript — so podcast audio could be edited simply by trimming words and lines to get the desired output. The learning curve is shallower, as the controls are organised around the script, but the tool still enables precision edits as you might achieve in a professional audio editing app.

The difference here is that the tools fit the workflow, the user doesn’t need to learn the tool to apply to their context, the tool has been adapted to fit the context and job to be done.

New opportunities

The real design opportunity is to organise the controls around the work people recognise, rather than the structure and burden of a complex existing application. Previously held back by higher build costs, AI assisted development is now making more of these focused product offerings viable.

This doesn’t mean spinning up disposable ad-hoc solutions with AI. The overserved segment is a potential entry point for these new tools, but these users still expect software to be well maintained and supported for them to adopt into their workflow.

Rather than asking if we can create a cheap Photoshop replacement, we should be asking, which user tasks are being awkwardly served, where do users need control and how can we give them that control without overwhelming them?

Further Reading

  • Playful wants the masses to start vibe coding — Fast Company, 5 November 2026
  • Automattic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coding apps amid a changing internet — TechCrunch, 9 November 2026
  • Writing code versus shipping code: Productivity effects across generations of AI coding tools — VOXEU / CEPR, 21 June 2026
  • ArtCraft App Suite — Suite of free, open-source creative and productivity tools

title: Every click has a price now. Who designs how that “feels”?
text:
Every click has a price now. Who designs how that “feels”?

As the all-you-can-eat AI era is ending, UX designers must adapt to a new reality

Since the democratization of AI, roughly by the end of 2022, companies sold access to their products for less than it costs them to run.

That didn’t last long.

Now, to try the latest models or pro versions of certain tools, users need to pay extra in tokens, which have unofficially become AI’s currency. More and more products are moving to credit- and usage-based pricing, meaning every action comes with a cost.

So how does that price show up on screen? A cost preview before you run a task or perhaps a credits meter in the corner? It might look like a small detail, but it can be the reason people keep using your product or move to a competitor.

Cost is a design material, like latency or error states, and it deserves the same care. Our task as designers is to make users feel in control… not like they’re watching a taxi meter run.

Budget anxiety and bill shock are UX failures

Evidence suggests AI bills are rising because we’re asking models to do much more. We use them to plan, research, write code and take complex actions on our behalf. Every step burns tokens at an unprecedented speed.

But, contrary to popular belief, tokens are getting cheaper. According to Silicon Data’s LLM Token Expenditure Index, the market was paying about $1 per million tokens in late September 2026. In May, when prices hit their highest point this year, it was around $2.

This is a phenomenon known as the Jevons paradox. When something gets cheaper to use, we find so many new uses for it that total consumption goes up.

For senior managers and executives, the end of subsidized AI plans is causing budget anxiety. If they want their teams to keep using AI tools, to work faster and to be more efficient in routine tasks, they’ll need to spend more on tokens (and maybe cut spending elsewhere).

As much as this is a challenge for business leaders, it’s also a major challenge for UX designers. For most of us, it’s the first time we need to design screens that warn users, in real time, that they’re running out of usage because of cost. Few messages feel more intrusive, or create more tension, than “Daily limit reached. Try again in 5 hours.”

Making this message sound friendlier (beware of passive-aggressiveness) is on product teams and, in particular, on designers. If users can see, step by step, what every action costs, the limit won’t feel like an ambush.

Show the price before the click

In April, GitHub announced that all Copilot plans would move to usage-based billing on June 1, 2026. Instead of counting requests, every plan would come with a monthly allowance of “AI Credits,” consumed according to the tokens each task burns. Copilot Pro+, for example, costs $39 a month and includes $39 in credits.

On paper, it sounds fair, given that you pay for what you use. In practice, though, it didn’t work out that well.

Within a day, developers were telling The Register they’d burned through a big chunk of their monthly credits in hours. One Pro+ user said two hours of work ate about 8% of their allowance. Another spent more than $6 on a single request. Many threatened to move to Anthropic, OpenAI or cheaper options like OpenRouter.

Running out of credits so fast hurt users, but for many, the worst part was not knowing the cost in advance. The cost of each request now depends on the model, the size of the request and how complex the answer is.

How do you show a price that’s so difficult to predict? Here’s a list of good practices that many organizations are implementing in their products, and that I’d call non-negotiable:

  • Put the estimate next to the button. Show what an action will cost before people commit and make it visible by default. If it hides behind a setting or a tooltip, most people will never see it.
  • Ask before the big ones. When a task looks expensive, or would eat most of what’s left, ask for a quick confirmation first.
  • Show what each task cost. In Replit, you can hover over a usage icon in the Agent tab to see what each checkpoint cost. Users can also set spending alerts and hard budget caps.
  • Warn early, so no one gets cut off mid-task. Claude Enterprise alerts admins at 75% and 90% of the spend limit, so they can raise it before anyone gets blocked in the middle of a task. Admins can also let users see their own spend and how close they are to their limit.
  • Let people set their own cap. A maximum per task or per session stops an agent from burning through a month’s budget in one go.

If you’ve designed your product to follow all of the above, you’ve got the basics covered.

Thinking a bit out of the box, here’s one idea I haven’t seen in any of the AI tools I use daily. (Disclaimer: AI moves so fast that by the time you read this, someone may have shipped it).

The idea came to me while using one of my favorite AI tools: I’d love it if the tool talked in my language. At the moment, whenever I’m running out of credits, I see a message like “1,180 credits left.” Honestly, I have no idea what that means for my week. Is it a lot? Is it enough to finish what I’m working on?

As a user, I’d feel less anxious if I received a message saying, “That’s enough for about three more prototypes like this one.” It’s the same information, but because it names the type of project I’m working on, I can plan with it and know how far I can go with what’s left. The more the product learns how you work, the more accurate that estimate can be.

Not every click needs AI

So far, we’ve talked about what users see on screen. However, the biggest cost decisions are made long before that, when product teams decide which features will use AI and which won’t.

Many companies are already assessing what they get back from their AI spend. According to an EY survey published in July, 98% of senior leaders whose companies use token-based AI tools said those costs have made them reconsider their approach.

I believe design teams can build a case for company-wide AI optimization. We map out how people use a product, step by step, so we’re well positioned to spot where AI genuinely adds value and where it only burns tokens.

To do that, we can start with two practices that fit into how we already work.

First, give every AI feature a cost budget. Say your team is designing a feature that summarizes customer calls. Before building it, agree on a limit, for example, $2 per user per month. Then design around that number. If testing shows it costs $5, change the design. Maybe summaries only run for calls longer than 10 minutes, or users ask for one instead of getting it automatically. Or this feature doesn’t need AI at all.

Second, add cost to design reviews. Today, when we review a feature, we check whether it’s easy to use and accessible. With AI features, we have one more question: how much does it cost every time someone uses it? A “regenerate” button, for example, can make a single task cost several times more if users keep clicking it. Designers can’t know those numbers on their own, so engineers need to share them while the design is still under review, before the feature goes live.

As I said at the beginning of the article, cost is a design material, and design leaders should treat it like one. If we don’t, someone else will decide where AI is headed, and we’ll be left designing the “Daily limit reached” messages, with no influence whatsoever on what causes them.

Price is part of the experience

At some point in their careers, designers have had to design a feature or product with price in mind. An e-commerce site, for instance, is built around price at every step. Other examples are a pricing page or a seasonal offer you show as a pop-up on your site.

In all of these cases, users checked the price only before buying something. With AI products (especially LLMs), the price is behind every action users take inside the product. And in many cases, it stays invisible until the bill arrives, or until they run out of tokens and can’t keep working.

Designers have to decide how that price “feels,” including the friction of not being able to finish a project in one go, and having to pay more or wait a few hours to get back to it. It’s a task that comes with a lot of responsibility for us, regardless of whether tokens get cheaper.

Think back to the last time you took a taxi and kept glancing at the meter, not enjoying the city views. That’s how lots of people use AI tools today, with one eye on their credits instead of on their work. Designers can help them enjoy the ride again.

Arin Bhowmick (@arinbhowmick) is Chief Design Officer at SAP, based in San Francisco, California. The above article is personal and does not necessarily represent SAP’s positions, strategies or opinions.
